newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: SOCCER SHOWCASE-BRAZIL EXCHANGE FLAIR FOR WORK RATE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-BRAZIL EXCHANGE FLAIR FOR WORK RATE.

text.p: Brazil can be expected to be tactically sound, ruthlessly efficent -- and dull -- at the next World Cup, judging from their coach's verdict on Sunday's 2-0 win over Paraguay.
"We were perfect," said Brazil coach Mario Zagallo after the Copa America quarter-final. "This is the type of football we are going to play in the World Cup."
Instead of the flair, artistry and all-out attack that sets pulses racing, the veteran coach has recently been talking of closing down spaces, playing compactly and working hard off the ball.
Last week he said: "I would rather win playing ugly football than lose playing attractive football. Efficiency in football is based on victories. Everyone wants to win and I'm no different."

On Sunday, he had many thinking they had been watching a different match when he said: "We put on a great exhibition. We were applied when we had the ball and we were applied when we didn't have the ball."
Brazil's game plan had been to drop back en masse and catch the Paraguayans on the counter-attack.
The tactics worked to perfection, with Ronaldo scoring two clinically-taken goals. But with so many talented individuals in the team, many feel that Brazil need not adopt a no-risk approach.

Zagallo's behaviour this week has been a strange about-turn by a man who only last month appealed to coaches worldwide to adopt a more adventurous approach. When he announced the Copa America squad, he complained that Brazil could not put on exhibitions when they confronted opponents who shut up shop.
But he appears to have been stung after Brazil lost 4-2 to Norway and conceded three goals against Italy and two against Mexico in recent games.
Paraguay, who lead the South American World Cup qualifying group and seem certain to go to France next year, created several chances despite missing five regular players.
But, perhaps not surprisingly for a team whose goalkeeper is one of their main attacking weapons, they lacked a killer punch.
Jose Luis Chilavert regularly scores from free-kicks and penalties. His remarkably accurate free-kicks upfield are one of Paraguay's most potent attacking weapons.
His second half penalty save, when he dived to his left to deny Ronaldo a hat-trick, also appeared to give his team mates new-found confidence and encouragement.
"I'm pleased with the way Paraguay played. I think that next year, we can perform well at the World Cup. We are not going just to participate," he said.
